prep.title: In the morning
prep.text: Best in the morning, ideally fasting — results compare better with earlier ones.

prep.title: Fasting 8–12 h
prep.text: Do not eat for 8–12 hours before the blood test. Plain water is fine; coffee, sweetened tea and chewing gum are not.

prep.title: Fasting · about 2 h
prep.text: Come fasting. The test takes about 2 hours: you drink the glucose solution and stay at the centre until the last blood sample.

prep.title: Morning, rested
prep.text: In the morning (07:30–09:00), after 15–30 minutes of rest, without stress or exercise beforehand.

prep.title: Timed to your cycle
prep.text: As your doctor advises — usually days 2–5 of the cycle for FSH, LH and oestradiol, around day 21 for progesterone.

prep.title: 48 h preparation
prep.text: For 48 hours before the test: no sexual intercourse, no cycling or strenuous exercise and no rectal examination.

prep.title: First morning urine
prep.text: First urine of the morning: wash the area, let the first part of the stream go and collect the midstream urine in a sterile container.

prep.title: Before antibiotics
prep.text: The sample is taken before starting antibiotics. If you are already taking one, ask your doctor when to give the sample.

prep.title: Fresh sample
prep.text: About the size of a walnut, in a sterile container, brought to the lab within 2 hours.

prep.title: Before eating
prep.text: In the morning, before eating, drinking or brushing your teeth; before starting antibiotics.

prep.title: Swab instructions
prep.text: Not during your period. For 24–48 hours before: no intercourse, no vaginal medicines and no douching.

faq.a: For specialist visits we recommend booking — by phone, WhatsApp or on the “Book an appointment” page. Reception replies and confirms the time. For lab tests, call us to ask about the best time to come.

faq.q: Do I need to fast before a blood test?
faq.a: For glucose, fats (cholesterol, triglycerides), iron and insulin — yes: 8–12 hours without food; plain water is fine. Many other tests need no fasting, but the morning is the best time. Every test in our catalogue shows its preparation.

faq.q: How much do the tests cost?
faq.a: Prices are available from reception. The quickest way: add the tests to “My list” and send it to us on WhatsApp, Viber or by e-mail — we will reply with the exact price.

faq.q: Do you take blood from small children?
faq.a: Yes — our paediatrics department and laboratory have worked together since 2011. Bring your child’s health booklet and any earlier results. A toy or something to drink after the blood test helps a lot.

faq.q: When and how do I get my results?
faq.a: It depends on the test: most blood tests are quicker than microbiology cultures, which take a few days. When you give the sample, the staff tell you when and how to collect your results.

faq.q: What should I bring to my visit?
faq.a: An ID document, your doctor’s referral if you have one, a list of the medicines you take and any earlier results. Use sterile containers for urine and stool samples.

faq.q: Should I stop my medicines before tests?
faq.a: Do not stop any medicine without talking to your doctor. For some tests (e.g. thyroid hormones) your doctor may ask you to take your medicine after the blood test. Tell us which medicines you take when you come.

faq.q: On which day of the cycle are hormone tests done?
faq.a: Usually days 2–5 of the cycle for FSH, LH and oestradiol and around day 21 for progesterone — but always as your gynaecologist advises.

faq.q: How do I collect a urine sample?
faq.a: First urine of the morning: wash the area with water, let the first part of the stream go and collect the midstream urine in a sterile container. For a urine culture, the sample is taken before starting antibiotics.
